topicName: OR Conditions, UNION vs. OR, and IN vs. EXISTS
content: [{"order":1,"type":"heading","text":"Mastering SQL Tuning: OR Conditions, UNION vs. OR, and IN vs. EXISTS"},{"order":2,"type":"paragraph","text":"When writing complex SQL queries, developers often face multiple ways to achieve the exact same logical result. However, from a database optimizer's perspective, the choice between using OR conditions, UNION, UNION ALL, IN, or EXISTS can dramatically impact performance. This tutorial explores the internals of these constructs and provides best practices for optimal SQL tuning."},{"order":3,"type":"heading","text":"1. Understanding OR Conditions and Index Access"},{"order":4,"type":"paragraph","text":"Using the OR operator in a WHERE clause tells the database engine that a row satisfies the condition if at least one of the criteria is met. While simple to write, OR conditions frequently prevent the optimizer from efficiently using indexes, leading to full table scans."},{"order":5,"type":"code","text":"SELECT * FROM employees WHERE department_id = 10 OR salary > 80000;"},{"order":6,"type":"paragraph","text":"If department_id and salary are indexed separately, the database may not be able to combine the B-Tree traversals efficiently in a single pass, resulting in an expensive table scan. To resolve this, modern cost-based optimizers use 'Concatenation' (similar to a UNION ALL), but older database versions or complex conditions may still struggle."},{"order":7,"type":"heading","text":"2. UNION vs. OR: When to Switch"},{"order":8,"type":"paragraph","text":"A common rewriting technique for sluggish OR queries is splitting them into separate queries combined with UNION or UNION ALL."},{"order":9,"type":"code","text":"SELECT employee_id, first_name, salary FROM employees WHERE department_id = 10 UNION ALL SELECT employee_id, first_name, salary FROM employees WHERE salary > 80000;"},{"order":10,"type":"bullet_point","text":"UNION ALL: Does not remove duplicates. It simply concatenates the result sets, making it extremely fast. Use this when you know the conditions are mutually exclusive or duplicate rows do not matter."},{"order":11,"type":"bullet_point","text":"UNION: Removes duplicate rows by performing an internal sort or hash distinct operation. This adds CPU and memory overhead."},{"order":12,"type":"paragraph","text":"Tuning Rule: If your OR query causes a full table scan and involves columns with independent indexes, rewriting it as a UNION ALL can force the optimizer to use indexes on each separate branch."},{"order":13,"type":"heading","text":"3. IN vs. EXISTS: Subquery Performance"},{"order":14,"type":"paragraph","text":"Filtering data based on a subquery can be done using the IN operator or the EXISTS operator. Though they often yield identical execution plans due to smart query rewrites by modern optimizers, fundamental differences remain."},{"order":15,"type":"subheading","text":"The IN Operator"},{"order":16,"type":"code","text":"SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id IN (SELECT customer_id FROM customers WHERE country = 'USA');"},{"order":17,"type":"paragraph","text":"Historically, IN evaluates the subquery first, builds a temporary result set, and then filters the outer query. It also handles NULL values carefully. If the subquery returns a NULL, the entire IN condition can evaluate to UNKNOWN."},{"order":18,"type":"subheading","text":"The EXISTS Operator"},{"order":19,"type":"code","text":"SELECT * FROM orders o WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM customers c WHERE c.customer_id = o.customer_id AND c.country = 'USA');"},{"order":20,"type":"paragraph","text":"EXISTS relies on semi-join logic. It evaluates the inner query for each row processed by the outer query and stops evaluating (short-circuits) as soon as the first matching row is found. This makes EXISTS exceptionally powerful for correlated subqueries involving large datasets."},{"order":21,"type":"heading","text":"Summary Tuning Best Practices"},{"order":22,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Always inspect the execution plan (EXPLAIN PLAN) before and after modifying OR to UNION."},{"order":23,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Prefer UNION ALL over UNION unless duplicate elimination is an explicit business requirement."},{"order":24,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Use EXISTS for correlated subqueries against large tables because of its short-circuit evaluation capability."},{"order":25,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Beware of NULL values when substituting NOT IN with NOT EXISTS, as their behavior with missing data differs significantly."}]
